newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Infotech accord within sight at world trade talks.
newsitem.headline: Infotech accord within sight at world trade talks.

text.p: A deal to liberalise trade in the world's $600 billion market for information technology was within grasp on Tuesday after a day of intense haggling, ministers and officials said.

Senior trade officials from the United States, European Union and Japan were upbeat about prospects for an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) they hope will crown the first ministerial meeting of the fledgling World Trade Organisation (WTO).

In a flurry of negotiations that lasted well into the night on Tuesday, the big trading powers made good progress narrowing their differences on the types of products to be covered and timing of tariff reductions, but officials said some details remained to be worked out.
At the same time, the United States, the European Union and Japan were redoubling efforts to sell the idea to their Asian trading partners.
Working level negotiators from countries interested in joining the technology accord were to hold a round of discussions even later on Tuesday night, a European Union spokesman said.
Earlier on Tuesday the heads of the EU and U.S. delegations emerged from a luncheon meeting with their Japanese and Canadian counterparts with positive predictions on an ITA.
"We are making a lot of progress and we hope to make further progress this afternoon," European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said,

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefksy said she concurred with Brittan's comments, but declined to say anything more on the proposed pact to eliminate tariffs on an estimated $600 billion of computer and telecommunications products by 2000.
"Nothing's for sure until we finish the negotiations, but it's certainly moving in a very positive direction right now," Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton said.
Brittan briefed the ministers of the 15 members of the European Union, on whose behalf he negotiates, about the day-long talks.
"There were some hesitations by some countries on specific points," European Commission spokesman Peter Guilford told reporters. "But nobody implied they were backing away from an ITA.
"So far so good, a few ifs and buts, but no undermining of the process," he added.
However, several Asian nations have voiced reservations, with Malaysia saying the goal of free commerce in infotech by the turn of the century is too ambitious.
Malaysia opposed negotiating the pact and said it did not see agreement by the close of this week's meeting on Friday.
"We did not come here to discuss the Information Technology Agreement," international trade and industry minister Rafidah Aziz said. "All negotiations should be done in Geneva."

The hope of U.S. and EU officials is that a successful ITA agreement in Singapore will build momentum for further trade liberalisation and spur negotiations on another pact to open up basic telephone services markets.
"If we don't reach agreement an ITA, it might undermine confidence in getting other agreements like telecoms," Guilford said.

The 128 full delegations from WTO member countries and ministers and officials from nearly 30 others waiting to be admitted to the organisation have heard ringing appeals for progress on a separate telecoms liberalisation pact.

Negotiators at WTO headquarters in Geneva are facing a deadline to finalise a deal among some 50 countries by mid-February after failing in an earlier bid last April when the United States pulled out of the talks.
This sector, heavily protected in many emerging economies, is estimated to be worth well over $500 billion annually.
